sources.title: Temporal Boundaries in Alsea
sources.author: Eugene Buckley
sources.publisher: Proceedings of the Berkeley Linguistics Society; online publisher Linguistic Society of America
sources.citation: Proceedings of the Fourteenth Annual Meeting of the Berkeley Linguistics Society, pp. 10–22.
sources.annotation: Proposes an analysis of how Alsea verbs mark events' beginnings, endings and resulting states. Comparisons with English translations show why context matters. Selected scanned pages, including the conclusion and source notes, were visually read; historical linguistic analysis does not establish contemporary speaker numbers.
sources.contentReviewScope: Actual scanned article, printed pp. 10–12 and 17–21 (full PDF pp. 2–4 and 9–13), visually read after rendering. Publisher cover and article metadata also inspected. Intervening pp. 13–16 and final notes/reference page 22 were not read.

inspectedSubresources.scope: Author, DOI,1988 proceedings and 10–22 range; portal lists publication date 1988-10-25. The source card conservatively records the proceedings year.

claimBlocks.text: Buckley examines how Alsea noun phrases identify a referent, express possession and mark relationships such as movement toward a place. His study follows small grammatical elements whose placement depends on phrase structure, including a marker that appears after different words as the phrase changes. He also identifies questions the available texts cannot settle. These patterns and proposed explanations offer a focused introduction to grammar, rather than a complete teaching course or a present-day language-use survey.

claimBlocks.suggestedSection: How an event unfolds in recorded Alsea
claimBlocks.text: Buckley’s study asks how Alsea verbs present an event’s beginning, end or resulting state. He argues that suffixes do more than correspond to English past-tense translations: context can make the same form appear differently in English. His comparison of earlier transcriptions and translations shows why wording in a translated text may conceal a grammatical distinction. This is a proposed analysis of recorded language, rather than evidence about present speakers or the continuity of Alsea families.

scopeAndIdentityNotes: These are two distinct scholarly analyses by the same author, substantially drawing on earlier Frachtenberg language records. They are not two new fieldwork projects or two independent community voices.
A historical paper's description of a language as extinct is not adopted as a claim that Alsea people disappeared, and it does not establish present-day speaker or learner numbers.
No claim is made here about a confirmed broad Penutian genetic classification, present tribal-government equivalence, contemporary fluency, or permission to reproduce recorded narratives.
Root's separate 1920 source and archive/finding-aid work are not duplicated as additional source cards in this packet.
coverageGaps: An accessible inspected phonology analysis is still needed; the originally suggested reconstruction paper remains unread.
Current community-led teaching, speaker/learner information and community preferences cannot be established from these 1980s studies.
Later scholarly revisions and disagreement were not surveyed in this two-work pass.
